title: Sport psychology
examples: How does being too nervous affect my game?
Can you explain what the inverted-U theory means?
What is the best way to set goals for training?

explain.say: Today we are learning about sport psychology concepts. We will look at how feelings affect performance.
Arousal refers to your level of emotional excitement or alertness. It is how awake you feel before an event.
The inverted-U theory suggests performance is best at a medium arousal level. Too low or too high is not ideal.
Goal setting helps focus your training efforts effectively. We use the SMART framework for good goals.

items: Measurable: Can be counted or tracked
Relevant: Matters to your overall goals

explain.say: For example, instead of saying run faster, make it specific. Say you will run one lap in under sixty seconds.
In real life, imagine you are taking a big exam. A low arousal might mean you are sleepy. A high arousal might mean you are panicking.

faq.q: What is the difference between arousal and anxiety?
faq.a: Arousal is just your general level of alertness. Anxiety is a specific feeling of worry or nervousness about something coming up.
asks: Is arousal the same as stress?
What is the feeling of being too awake?

faq.q: Why is the optimal arousal level so important for athletes?
faq.a: Being in the optimal zone helps you perform consistently. It means you are awake enough to focus but calm enough to think clearly.
asks: What happens if I am too relaxed?
Does performance drop if I am nervous?

faq.q: Can I use the SMART method for non-sport goals too?
faq.a: Yes, the SMART framework is very useful everywhere. You can use it to plan for studying or even managing your time.
asks: Are SMART goals only for sports?
How do I make a goal measurable?

faq.q: If I am too anxious, what can I do to bring my arousal down?
faq.a: Deep breathing exercises are a good technique. They help to calm your breathing and signal to your body that you are safe.
asks: What calms me down before a race?
What is a physical way to lower arousal?

asks: Is achievable the same as easy?
How do I check if a goal is achievable?

facts: Arousal is a measure of physiological excitement.
The inverted-U theory suggests an optimal zone exists.
SMART goals must be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.
Deep breathing is a technique to manage high arousal.

quiz.say: If an athlete feels extremely calm before a competition, their arousal level is likely:
quiz.why: Low arousal might mean you are too relaxed to perform at your best.

wrong.0: High arousal suggests too much excitement or panic.
wrong.1: Arousal cannot be zero; some level of alertness is always present.
wrong.3: Medium is the optimal zone, but the question describes a low state.

quiz.say: Which component of SMART goals ensures the goal has a finish line?
quiz.why: Time-bound means setting a clear deadline for when the goal must be met.

wrong.0: Measurable tells you how to track progress, not the deadline.
wrong.1: Relevant checks if the goal matters to you, not when it must happen.
wrong.3: Specific describes what the goal is, not when it ends.

quiz.say: A goal to improve your free throw percentage from seventy percent to eighty percent by the end of the month is:
quiz.why: This goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.

wrong.1: It is too vague and lacks a clear end date.
wrong.2: It misses the measurable and time-bound elements.
wrong.3: It fails to state why this goal is important to the student.
